cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve?
cards.answer: The empirical finding, first measured by Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) via self-experiments on nonsense syllables, that memory retention decays steeply with time when no attempt is made to retain it — newly learned material roughly halves within days or weeks absent review.

cards.heading: Key mechanism
cards.question: How did Ebbinghaus quantify retention in his experiments?
cards.answer: As 'savings' — the reduction in time needed to relearn material compared with the time needed to learn it the first time — fitted with a logarithmic decay formula.

cards.heading: Shape of the curve
cards.question: What shape does retention loss take over time, per the Ebbinghaus curve?
cards.answer: Steepest immediately after learning, then flattening out over time.

cards.heading: Replication
cards.question: How did a 2015 replication of Ebbinghaus's 1885 self-experiment turn out?
cards.answer: It reproduced results similar to the original data — notable durability for a 140-year-old self-experiment.

cards.heading: Scope of the original finding
cards.question: Did Ebbinghaus's original work study the effect of spaced review, or only the forgetting itself?
cards.answer: Only the forgetting itself. Spaced repetition — scheduling review at increasing intervals to counteract the curve — is a derivative practice that came later, built on his curve as its empirical foundation.
